_note: Atlas rows this archive has READ and judged to be ONE PLACE, with the reason
TWO KINDS OF GROUP LIVE HERE, and the second was added on the evening of the
21st after the first pass reported them as identical-coordinate tidying and
they were not. The measurement that said so had excluded inherited pins before
measuring, then the result was described as being about all the rows — a
number correctly computed, about something adjacent to the claim made for it,
which is the fault this archive spent the day naming.
ONE PLACE, TWO SPELLINGS. Italia and Italy, Inglaterra, AU for Australia, a
capital letter. Both rows sit on the same point and nothing is being
corrected — only the weight, which was split between them.
ONE PLACE, AND ONE OF THE ROWS IS STANDING ON A BORROWED PIN. Berkeley was
two rows: six people on the geocode for the word ENGLAND and two on Berkeley
in Gloucestershire. Folding them is not tidying. It moves six people a
hundred and twenty-four kilometres onto the place they are actually from.
WHICH ROW SURVIVES IS A JUDGEMENT AND IS STATED EVERY TIME. Where one row's
pin is demonstrably the place, it wins however few people it holds — the two
-person Berkeley row keeps its coordinate and the six-person row folds into
it. Where NO row's pin is the place, the survivor is the one that ADMITS it:
Ehrstaedt keeps the row marked `parent` on Heidelberg over one claiming to be
approximate a hundred and forty kilometres from the district its own string
names.
beside each. A neighbouring archive, building a graves layer over this map on
21 September 2026, found twenty place-heads appearing more than once and four
of them at different coordinates. It did not merge any of them, correctly:
whether two Hornby Castles are one castle is a question for somebody who has
read the deeds, not for a deduplication script.
THE RULE THIS FILE ENFORCES IS: one head, one place, one pin. Two rows whose
head is the same name and whose pins are more than two kilometres apart are
either one place geocoded twice or two places sharing a name, and the archive
must say which. check_atlas.py refuses a build where such a pair exists and is
not settled here.
HOW A FOLD IS DONE, AND WHY IT CANNOT LOSE ANYBODY. `keep` is the row that
survives, chosen as the one holding the most people so that its head, its slug
and its page do not change — the Booyzen archive warned that a hand-pinned
place silently loses its people when its head changes, and that is the trap
here. Each folded string is added to the kept row's VARIANTS, and atlas.py
already gathers a row's people by looking up its name and every variant. So
the people follow the string rather than the row, and nobody is dropped.
NOTHING HERE MOVES A MARKER. A fold says two rows name one place; it does not
claim the surviving pin is in the right spot. Where the kept pin is itself only
approximate it stays flagged approximate.

groups.head: Hornby Castle
fold: Hornby Castle, North Riding, Yorkshire, England
groups.why: ONE CASTLE, THREE GEOCODES, AND THE PEOPLE SETTLE IT. All three strings name a castle in Yorkshire, and the nine people spread across them are one circle: Conyers D'Arcy «of Hornby Castle», the 1st Earl of Holderness who was 8th Lord Darcy de Knayth and 5th Lord Conyers, Dorothy Bellasyse, Elizabeth Conyers, and Thomas and Grace Rokeby. This archive's own /hornby page states the seat: Hornby Castle in the NORTH RIDING of Yorkshire, held by the Conyers and then the Earls of Holderness from the 1560s. The kept pin, 54.338 -1.654, is that castle. The other two are artefacts: 53.715 -0.501 is in the EAST Riding, on the wrong side of the county from the string's own «North Riding»; and 54.288 -1.591 is Bedale itself — the town the string named to disambiguate the castle became the answer instead of the castle. There is a second Hornby Castle in Lancashire, in the Lune valley, and it is not what any of these three strings says.

groups.head: Langdon Hall
groups.why: THE COUNTY WAS WRITTEN AS ITS COUNTY TOWN AND THE PIN WENT TO CUMBRIA. «Langdon Hall, Warwick, England» is 54.900 -2.839 — near Brampton, two hundred and ninety-nine kilometres from the Warwickshire row and in a different half of the country. The four people are one household across one generation: Thomas Dabridgecourt born 1531, Alice Griswold born 1535, Katherine Dabridgecourt born 1556 who died there, and John Fullwood born 1563 who also died there — and it is John Fullwood alone who carries the Cumbrian string. The tree names the man himself «Thomas DABRIDGECOURT of LONGDON Hall» while recording his birthplace as LANGDON Hall, so the archive's own data carries two spellings of one seat.

groups.head: Heidelberg
groups.why: THE PALATINATE, FILED UNDER THE KINGDOM THAT SWALLOWED IT TWO CENTURIES LATER. The folded row is 49.952 12.390, in Bavaria near the Czech border, and the man on it is ELECTOR PALATINE CHARLES LOUIS VON DER PFALZ — Karl I Ludwig, whose seat was Heidelberg on the Neckar and whose court is the reason this archive has any Heidelberg at all. «Deutschland(HRR)» is the Holy Roman Empire and «Bayern» is the Rhenish Palatinate's administration after 1816, a hundred and ninety-nine years after the 1617 date on the row. The gazetteer read the later region and found a Heidelberg inside it. Every Heidelberg string here dates 1610-1617 and belongs to one court.

groups.head: Averham
groups.why: THE SAME COUNTY-TOWN FAULT, TWENTY-FOUR KILOMETRES OF IT. «Averham, NOTTINGHAM, England» lands on Nottingham city at 52.953 -1.150; Averham is a parish near Newark at 53.083 -0.860, which is where the other two rows sit. The seven people are one family — Robert Ambrose Sutton, William Sutton, Mary St Leger and Bridget Sutton, the Suttons of Averham — and Bridget is alone on the Nottingham pin. «UK» against «England» is the third row and is not a different country. Averham Park is left as its own place: it is the park beside the parish and has a separate head.

groups.head: Market Bosworth
groups.why: COUNTY TOWN AGAIN, AND A CAPITALISATION. «MARKET BOSWORTH, LEICESTER, England» lands on Leicester city at 52.636 -1.133, eighteen kilometres from Market Bosworth at 52.624 -1.402. The third row differs from the kept one only by «, UK.» on the end. The three people — William Noel, Elizabeth Dixie and Frances de Beaumont — are the Dixies of Bosworth Hall and the Noels, one Leicestershire circle in one town. Bosworth Hall keeps its own row: it is a house in the town rather than another name for it.

groups.head: Limerick
groups.verdict: one city, and the gap is not a disagreement
groups.why: Fifteen hundred metres is a gazetteer answering the same question twice, not two Limericks. Both rows are the city; twelve people were split between them, including Richard Atkinson and Mary Bowen appearing on BOTH — which is what a split head does to a roster. «Limerick City, Ireland» and «ST. MARY'S, Limerick» keep their own rows: different heads, and St Mary's is the cathedral this archive has an actual record from.

groups.head: Cork
groups.verdict: one city, and the gap is not a disagreement
groups.why: A kilometre apart in the same city. The kept row carries the exact fix. «County Cork, Ireland» is NOT folded — that is the county, a genuinely broader place, and merging it into the city would be the very fault this map was just corrected for.

groups.head: Berkeley
groups.why: **THE ONE THAT MATTERS.** «Berkeley, **Gloucester**, England» — the county written as its county town again — failed to geocode and took the pin for the word ENGLAND, 52.531 -1.265, near Lindley in Leicestershire. Six people sat on it, marked exact, for weeks: this archive's central place, in the wrong county, on the map of an archive that is largely about Berkeley. The other row is the real parish at 51.691 -2.459 and holds two. Folding puts **all eight on Berkeley**, a hundred and twenty-four kilometres from where six of them were. The two-person row keeps its coordinate because its coordinate is right; headcount does not enter into it.

groups.head: London
groups.why: «London, Middlesex, England» is on the England point with two people. «London, England» is on London at 51.507 -0.128 with one. Middlesex is the historic county London sat in and is not a different city.

groups.head: Toowoomba
groups.verdict: one town, five rows, and the 955-kilometre one folded with them
groups.why: The row the original report flagged — 955 km out at -22.165 144.584 — is «Toowoomba, **Toowoomba Region**, Queensland, Australia» sitting on the QUEENSLAND centroid, and the extra administrative level is what defeated the lookup. Three more rows are already on Toowoomba proper. The fifth, «Toowoomba Q'ld  Australia», carries **no comma at all**, so its head is the whole string and it never appeared in any duplicate-head count — which is worth knowing about every head-based measurement on this map.

groups.head: St Quivox
groups.verdict: the parish, not the county town
groups.why: «St Quivox, **Ayr**, Scotland» borrowed Ayr's pin at the round number 55.5 -4.5; the parish is at 55.484 -4.572, five kilometres off. Ayr is the town, Ayrshire the county, and the parish is neither.

groups.head: St. James Palace
groups.keep: St. James Palace, London, Middlesex, Englan
fold: St. James Palace, London, Middlesex, England, Kingdom of England
groups.verdict: the palace, on a row with a truncated word in it
groups.why: The surviving string ends «Englan», cut off in the export. It is kept anyway, because **it is the row whose pin is the palace** — 51.504 -0.139 — while the tidier-looking one, which ends «Kingdom of England», is on the England centroid a hundred and thirty-eight kilometres away. A better-spelled string is not a better coordinate.

groups.head: Ehrstaedt
groups.verdict: neither pin is the village, and one of them says so
groups.why: **The exception to the rule above, and the reason the rule is stated rather than coded.** One row is marked `approx` at 48.193 8.139; the other is marked `parent` on Heidelberg. The approx pin is **141 km from the Heidelberg its own string names**, which is not an approximation of anything. So the survivor is the row that admits it is standing on Heidelberg's point rather than the row claiming a precision it does not have. The village keeps no coordinate of its own here, which is the honest end state until somebody finds one.

groups.head: Arienzo
groups.why: Same point, same town, one word in two languages. Twelve people and two.

groups.head: Brisbane
groups.verdict: one city, three depths of address
groups.why: Same point three times: the bare city, the city with its state, and the city with state and country. Twenty people, one and one.

groups.head: Caserta
groups.why: Same point, one word in two languages.

groups.head: Keele
groups.why: Same point. The second row has the county and the country run together with a hyphen and the country in Spanish, which is what a tree exported through more than one language does.

groups.head: Rockhampton
groups.why: Same point.

groups.head: Santa Maria a Vico
groups.keep: Santa Maria a Vico, Caserta, Campania, Italia
fold: Santa Maria A Vico, Nola, Terra Di Lavoro
groups.why: Same point. **Terra di Lavoro** is the historic province the town sat in before Caserta, and Nola is the diocese — an older address for one place rather than a second place.

groups.head: Ashton under Hill
groups.why: Same point, and **both rows are on Gloucestershire's pin** — so this fold corrects the weight and nothing else. The village still has no coordinate of its own and the surviving row still says so. Two further rows, «Ashton Underhill, Gloucester, England» and «Ashton, Underhill, Gloucestershire, England», are almost certainly the same village under different HEADS; they are left alone here and noted on the work list, because folding across heads is a wider decision than this register was opened for.
